title: Move all zeros to the end while preserving order (two-pointer swap).
shortTitle: Move All Zeros to the End While Preserving Order
keyPoints: A write pointer collects non-zero values at the front in order; the remaining tail is filled with zeros
The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, modifying the array in place
Stability is critical: non-zero values must keep their original relative order
The two-pass write-and-fill approach is the easiest to reason about and minimizes writes when zeros are frequent
The one-pass swap variant moves zeros rightward as it goes but does more writes on mostly-non-zero arrays
This is a stable partition around a predicate: the same pattern works for any condition, not just zero

s1_definition.oneliner: A write pointer collects non-zeros in order at the front; then fill the rest with zeros at the end.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two-pointer compaction** – a write pointer tracks where the next non-zero goes, and a scan pointer walks the entire array.
- **Stability** – the non-zero values keep their original relative order, making this a stable partition.
- **In-place** – no extra array is allocated; only two index variables are used.
- **Two-pass version** – pass 1 copies non-zeros forward; pass 2 fills the tail with zeros.
- **One-pass swap version** – swaps non-zeros into position as it scans, moving zeros rightward.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a row of settlement slots for Rajesh's day where some carry a real amount and some are empty (zero). The bank wants all real amounts compacted to the front in the same order they occurred, with the empty slots pushed to the back. A clerk keeps one finger on the next front slot and scans every slot; each real amount is slid forward, and whatever is left becomes empty.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Moving all zeros to the end while preserving order is a two-pointer in-place algorithm. I keep a write pointer for the next front position and scan the whole array. Every non-zero value I find gets placed at the write position, and after the scan I fill the remaining positions with zeros. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

The requirement I never lose sight of is stability: the non-zero values must keep their original relative order. Both the write-and-fill and the swap approaches preserve order because they process left to right and never reorder two non-zeros. A faster two-ends approach would scramble the order, which breaks the requirement.

The pattern generalizes beyond zeros. It is really a stable partition around a predicate: replace the non-zero test with any condition and the same code pushes failing elements to the end while keeping the rest in order. For money at the National Bank of India, I use `BigDecimal` and test with `signum()` rather than `==`.

A small but important optimization skips the store when the write and scan pointers are equal, avoiding redundant self-writes on a mostly-non-zero array. This reduces memory traffic on large batch arrays where the real data far outnumbers the zeros.

Remember one sentence: a write pointer collects non-zeros at the front in order, the tail is filled with zeros, and the result is a stable in-place partition in linear time.
